label: map_1
name: Self-Memoizing Depth Cache
mech: Each token first passes through a 4-layer fast path. A learned locality-sensitive hash of its residual state then queries a RAM-resident table of up to about 1B int8 entries. Each entry stores a compressed delta ("this is what layers 5–24 would have added"). On a confident hit the 20 deep layers are skipped and the delta is added. On a miss the slow path runs and its delta is written back as a new entry. Training does three things together: it distills the slow path into the cache entries, it shapes the hash so that states with similar deltas share buckets, and it calibrates a hit-confidence gate. Lookups cost bytes rather than FLOPs, so the 32 GB of RAM becomes stored computation, and PCIe only carries the few kilobytes each token needs.
value: Effective depth and throughput keep improving with use and data seen, not with parameters, so a fixed-FLOP transformer cannot match it on recurring computations.

label: map_1
name: Foreign-Neuron Retrieval Model
mech: Every feed-forward neuron of a frozen open 7B–13B model is extracted as a (key, value) pair and quantized to 4 bits. The roughly 2B-vector index lives in RAM, behind a product-quantized nearest-neighbour index. A trainable 200M "host" model learns per-layer projections from its own residual into the teacher's residual coordinates. With those it retrieves the top 2–8k neurons for each token, applies the teacher's activation function to those neurons only, and maps the summed values back into its own stream. The projections are trained by distillation: the retrieval-augmented output has to match the full teacher's output. The neuron selection is made differentiable through a straight-through top-k. Each token then costs only a few megabytes of RAM reads and about 2% of the teacher's feed-forward FLOPs.
value: The model gets close to a 7–13B model's factual and associative capacity while training and running at roughly the compute and VRAM cost of a 200M model.

label: map_1
name: Sleep-Consolidated Growing Slots
mech: While the model is in use, any token span with high loss or user correction is stored in a RAM episodic buffer as compact latent states plus targets. During idle hours the GPU replays these episodes into a pool of sparse weight "slots": small rank-4 adapters keyed by a content hash, with up to millions of them in RAM. A slot is allocated only when its gradient conflicts with existing slots (measured as gradient cosine below zero), so new learning goes into new capacity instead of overwriting old capacity. While the model runs, a router loads only the 8–32 slots that match the current context into VRAM. The dense core stays mostly frozen, with interleaved replay from a reservoir sample of old episodes.
value: The model keeps learning new facts and skills indefinitely after deployment without catastrophic forgetting or full retraining, while a same-budget transformer is fixed after its weekly training run.

label: map_2
name: Chunk-Paged RAM Expert Ocean
mech: A 150M-parameter GPU core is paired with a bank of about 60,000 int8 low-rank expert blocks (rank-64 deltas for every core layer, about 15B parameters, about 15 GB) held in system RAM. A cheap pass over each 1,024-token chunk produces a product-key query that selects 64 experts for the whole chunk, not per token. Their roughly 250 MB of weights stream over PCIe (about 10 ms) while the previous chunk computes, using double buffering. In training, the GPU returns gradients only for the selected experts, and the CPU applies them with a factorized Adafactor-style optimizer whose state is a tiny fraction of the bank. The bank's FLOP cost per token therefore equals a 200M model's, while its stored capacity is about 75 times larger.
value: It gives the knowledge and skill capacity of a roughly 15B-parameter model at the training and inference compute of a 200M one, which a dense same-budget transformer cannot store at all.

label: map_2
name: Corpus-Indexed Residual Language Model
mech: The full training corpus, plus any user documents, is kept in RAM as a compressed FM-index (about 5 GB for 5B tokens). For every position, the CPU finds the longest matching suffix in the corpus and returns its continuation statistics: the top-16 next tokens with counts, the match length and the source offsets. These go into the network as input embeddings and as an additive logit prior. The network is trained only on the loss of the mixture, so its gradients go entirely to what exact lookup cannot predict: generalization, composition and paraphrase. Memorization moves out of the weights into an index the CPU queries for free, alongside the GPU.
value: It recalls billions of tokens verbatim with sources and absorbs new text instantly by appending to the index, with no retraining. A same-budget transformer must spend most of its 200M weights memorizing, and does so lossily.

label: map_2
name: Fast-Weight Episodic Cortex with Sleep
mech: Each attention layer carries rank-16 fast weights that are updated during inference by one gradient step per chunk on the model's own next-token loss. This is cheap because only about 1M parameters change, so effective context becomes unbounded and is held in weights rather than a KV cache. When the PC is idle, a "sleep" phase replays logged episodes. It distills fast weights that kept being useful into new or existing experts in the Idea 1 RAM bank, using a frozen 4-bit open-weight 7B model (about 5 GB) as a regularizing teacher to prevent drift and forgetting. A meta-learned learning-rate and gating network, trained offline on document sequences, decides what gets written and what gets consolidated.
value: The model keeps learning permanently from its owner's daily use on the same hardware, with no context-length limit and no catastrophic forgetting. A trained-once, frozen same-budget transformer cannot do this.

label: map_3
name: Co-Access Paged Host Memory
mech: A 200M-parameter GPU controller is paired with a sparse key-value memory of about 20B int8 rows kept in the 32 GB of host RAM. Rows are grouped into 64 KB pages. A cheap first pass over each 256-token chunk predicts which pages the chunk needs, about 64 pages or 4 MB. That set is copied over PCIe 4.0 (about 25 GB/s) while the GPU is still working on the previous chunk, so the transfer time is hidden. During training, only the rows that were touched get gradients, and CPU threads apply sparse Adam updates to them in RAM. Every night a CPU job re-clusters rows into pages using the co-access graph, so each page fetch serves many tokens. This keeps bandwidth use high while VRAM holds only the controller and the active pages.
value: It gives the model a 20B-parameter knowledge store at the per-token compute cost of a 200M model, a capacity no dense same-budget transformer can hold in 12 GB.

label: map_3
name: Frozen-Prior Surprise Delta Model
mech: An open-weight 3B model quantized to 4-bit (about 2 GB VRAM) stays frozen and supplies a prior distribution plus hidden states at every position. The trainable network is a small recurrent side model (about 150M parameters). It reads those hidden states and outputs only a gated additive correction to the prior's logits. It is trained only on high-loss tokens, where the prior's loss is high and the corrected output could still improve. These tokens are found by running the frozen prior forward once at inference cost, and they are about 15% of the corpus. At inference a learned gate skips the side model on confident tokens, and on those tokens the prior's later layers exit early. As a result, the backward pass and most FLOPs go only to new information.
value: The 5B-token weekly budget acts like roughly 30B tokens of useful signal on top of a stronger prior, without ever paying training cost for what the prior already knows.

label: map_3
name: Idle-Time Sleep Consolidation
mech: During use, the model writes episodic traces into a ring buffer in RAM: the context, its own outputs, user corrections and high-surprise spans. When the PC is idle, a "sleep" job replays these traces mixed with samples from its normal training data, which guards against forgetting. Any rewritten answers produced during replay are checked by the frozen open-weight model from Idea 2 before they are kept. The job then distils the result into the memory pages of Idea 1 and the side model's low-rank adapters. Updates are confined to sparse rows and adapters. That keeps a nightly session to a few GPU-hours and makes it reversible: the job keeps checkpoints, and a validation probe rolls back any update that hurts held-out perplexity.
value: The model keeps learning the owner's documents and tasks on the same PC indefinitely, while a same-budget transformer stays frozen at the end of training.

label: g1_neg
name: Typed Relational State Machine
mech: Next to a small transformer, the model keeps an explicit per-context graph of at most 64 entity slots, each with a typed attribute vector, plus a sparse relation matrix between slots. At each token a small controller emits discrete edit operations: create, bind, update attribute, add or remove relation, or no-op. These are trained with straight-through Gumbel estimates, so next-token loss reaches the operations through a graph readout that the decoder attends to. A small auxiliary loss rewards edits that make later references predictable, such as pronouns, quantities and possession changes. The graph is a few kilobytes per sequence and the controller adds about 5% compute, so this fits easily on a 3060.
value: It gives exact, length-independent tracking of entities and state (who holds what after 40 transfers), which a 200M transformer can only approximate in its attention patterns and loses as the context grows.

label: g1_neg
name: Counterfactually Factorized Hidden State
mech: The residual stream is split into named subspaces such as tense, number, speaker, topic, numeric value and polarity. Training adds interchange-intervention losses: the model runs on a pair of inputs that differ in one factor, the matching subspace is swapped between the two runs, and the output must change exactly as the counterfactual text predicts. The counterfactual pairs are generated on the CPU by templated and rule-based perturbations of the corpus, for example number inflection, entity swaps and digit edits. That costs nothing on the GPU, and roughly every third training batch is a paired batch.
value: The model generalises systematically, recombining factors in ways it never saw together, and it can be edited reliably by setting a subspace directly. An unconstrained same-budget transformer only gets there with far more data.

label: g1_neg
name: Bidirectional Joint-Likelihood Consistency
mech: One shared network is trained to factorise each sequence both left-to-right and right-to-left, with a learned direction embedding selecting the order. A consistency loss penalises any disagreement between the two total sequence log-likelihoods, which must be equal for a coherent joint distribution. Disagreement on a sequence also flags it as a high-information sample, and those samples are reweighted in later epochs. The cost is about 1.6 times the compute per token, but every token gives two prediction targets plus a consistency constraint, which raises data efficiency within the 5B-token weekly budget.
value: It removes the reversal curse ("A is B" implies "B is A") and gives better-calibrated probabilities over whole sequences, which a one-directional transformer trained on the same budget cannot achieve.

label: g1_core
name: LDPC-Coded Fact Memory
mech: Facts are stored as sparse binary words (8192 bits, 64 active). Together they form the null space of a large sparse constraint graph held in host RAM (10-20 GB of edge lists), learned incrementally with a Karbasi-style null-space rule over spans the model encodes from the corpus. At chosen layers the model emits a noisy partial word from its hidden state. The CPU runs 5-10 rounds of min-sum decoding to reach the nearest stored codeword, and a learned projection adds that codeword back into the residual stream. The query head is trained with a straight-through estimator. Decoding is sparse integer work on the CPU that overlaps with GPU compute, so capacity grows with code length rather than VRAM.
value: It recalls whole facts from corrupted or half-given cues, at a capacity well beyond what 200M dense weights hold.

label: g1_core
name: Incremental-Smoothing Weight Estimation
mech: Weight blocks (heads, FFN slabs) are treated as SLAM variables. Each batch adds a linearized factor (Kronecker-factored information plus residual) to a sparse square-root information matrix kept in fp32 in host RAM. Cross-block factors are kept only between blocks that are strongly co-activated. A Bayes tree updates only the affected cliques. A block's Jacobians are recomputed on a stored mini-sample only when its estimate drifts past a threshold; otherwise it is solved by cheap back-substitution. The GPU computes forward passes and Jacobian sketches, and the CPU does the sparse Cholesky updates. Each token's information is kept rather than fading out through momentum.
value: It reaches a target loss on far fewer tokens than first-order training, which matters most when data is the binding limit.

label: g1_core
name: Difference-Map Constraint Reasoning
mech: A slot-based reasoning latent x is refined by Elser's difference map: x <- x + beta[P_A(f_B(x)) - P_B(f_A(x))]. P_A is a small transformer that projects onto logically consistent states. P_B projects onto knowledge-consistent states through Idea 1's decoder or a layer of a frozen quantized open model. Both are trained with an idempotence loss plus task loss, using implicit differentiation at the fixed point, so memory use stays constant however many iterations run. Iteration stops when the two projections agree. Each step is cheap enough to run hundreds of times on the 3060.
value: It solves constraint-heavy multi-step problems where single-pass or single-loop models get stuck at wrong fixed points.

label: g1_core2
name: Helmert-Blocked Closed-Form Training
mech: A briefly trained 120M trunk is frozen, and above it sits a head of 4096 cells, each a 512×256 linear map. Each token is routed to one cell by k-means on the trunk state, and every cell maps into a shared 256-d vocabulary factor taken from a PCA of a 1.5B open model's logits. The head is trained in one streaming pass: for each token, the GPU adds rank-1 updates to that cell's normal equations (XᵀX, and XᵀY where Y is the teacher's logits in the PCA basis), which take about 6 GB. The cell unknowns are removed by Schur complement onto the shared factor, which is solved by Cholesky; the cells are then back-substituted, and two or three such alternations replace SGD entirely.
value: The head reaches the exact least-squares optimum without backward passes, learning rates or activation memory, so it takes in several times more tokens per week than a backprop-trained model of the same size.

label: g1_core2
name: Motion-Compensated KV Coding
mech: The context is split into 64-token chunks grouped into GOPs. I-chunks keep their full fp16 K/V. Each P-chunk stores, per head, a motion vector (a reference chunk plus token alignment, found by matching key sketches) and a quantized low-rank residual. An encoder chooses between I and P coding and sets the residual rank by Lagrangian rate-distortion optimization, with distortion measured as attention-output error on probe queries. Attention rebuilds P-chunks from their references in shared memory, so the GPU mostly reads small residuals.
value: Repetitive material such as code, logs and long documents gets million-token working memory in 12 GB, with every token still exactly addressable where a same-budget transformer would have to truncate or evict.

label: g1_core2
name: Merit-Order Compute Dispatch
mech: Three units share one tokenizer: a 200M student (baseload), a 1.5B open model (mid-merit) and a 4-bit 8B open model (peaker). A 5M forecaster reads the student's hidden state and predicts how much each unit would reduce loss over the next 16 tokens; it is trained by regression on logged realized reductions. A dual price λ is updated by subgradient so that compute spending clears the latency budget. A unit is committed only when its forecast gain is larger than λ times its running cost plus its startup cost (catch-up prefill of the tokens it skipped). A minimum up-time keeps the 8B's KV cache warm across hard spans, and it is idled across easy ones.
value: It delivers near-8B quality on the hard tokens at about 2-3× the cost of the small model, a cost-quality point that no single same-budget transformer can reach.

label: g1_mech
name: Seed-Regrown Weight Blocks
mech: Each large weight matrix is never stored. It is rebuilt on the chip, block by block, as a weighted sum of K pseudorandom matrices, each fully determined by a 32-bit integer seed, plus a small dense correction. The card regenerates a block's values from a counter hash inside fast on-chip memory just before it multiplies with that block. Only the seeds, the mixing coefficients and the small correction are stored and updated by the prediction-error signal. Every few thousand steps, seeds whose coefficients have stayed near zero are swapped for fresh random seeds, so the basis is gradually searched rather than fixed. The card does about 70 arithmetic operations for every byte it can fetch, so trading spare arithmetic for scarce memory traffic and storage lets a network with roughly 10-20B virtual weights train and run in 12 GB, with update bookkeeping about 1000 times smaller.
value: The width and depth of the network are set by the arithmetic budget instead of the 12 GB memory ceiling, which a stored-weight model of the same budget cannot escape.

label: g1_mech
name: Reducibility-Priced Text Diet
mech: Before training, a frozen 4-bit open-weight model makes one pass over the corpus and stores one number per 512-piece span in RAM: its own prediction error, in bits per piece. During training, the CPU keeps a short history of the small model's error on each span. It then computes two things: the gap (small error minus frozen error) and the slope (how fast that gap has shrunk over recent visits). Spans are sampled in proportion to gap times slope. Spans where even the frozen model's error is high are treated as noise and dropped, and spans whose gap has closed are retired. The frozen model never touches the small model's outputs or internal states. It only sets prices, so the weekly 5B-piece budget goes to content that can be learned but has not been learned yet.
value: Each week's compute buys several times more learnable signal per piece than a model that sees the corpus uniformly or by plain error ranking.

label: g1_mech
name: Backward-Recovery Self-Audit
mech: One shared stack of layers feeds two readouts: one predicts the next piece left to right, and the other predicts the previous piece right to left. They are trained jointly on reversed and unreversed copies of the same spans, at almost no extra memory cost. During generation, the system samples several candidate continuations. For each one it measures how many bits the right-to-left readout needs to recover the prompt from that continuation, and it keeps the candidate that needs the fewest. During training, positions where the two directions assign strongly different probabilities to the same middle span get extra weight. This pushes the shared layers to hold facts that work in both directions instead of one-way surface habits. All of this fits easily on a 12 GB card, because the second readout is small and the checking is batched candidate passes.
value: The model gets a built-in signal for spotting continuations that aren't supported by the prompt, and a forward-only model of the same size has no internal way to compute that.

label: g1_loop
name: Wahlund-Split Factorized Decoder
mech: The 64k vocabulary is arranged as a 256×256 grid. A ~150M local-context network predicts the row and column codes independently, conditioned on a deme chosen by a binary router tree, and each leaf of the tree owns a small low-rank modulation. The CPU keeps a joint-count table for each leaf in RAM (a few hundred MB) and computes the heterozygote-deficit statistic F from joint versus product-of-marginal frequencies. A leaf with significant F is split by 2-means over its routed hidden states, with the child adapters copied from the parent. Sibling leaves with F_ST ≈ 0 are merged. Two 256-way softmaxes replace the 64k softmax, which frees compute and VRAM for the base network.
value: Output capacity and the number of experts grow exactly where the cheap independence assumption fails, so the model gets a large-vocabulary decoder for a fraction of the cost of a full softmax.

label: g1_loop
name: Granger-Wired Lag Heads
mech: The base model attends only within a 256-token window, so it is fast and small. Periodically the CPU runs Granger F-tests on logged batches. For each pair of hidden-state cluster (out of 1024 k-means codes) and lag band, it tests whether that cluster appearing in that band explains variance in the current per-token surprisal residual, with Bonferroni correction. Each significant pair creates a "wire": a single-query head that attends only to the positions where that cluster fired inside that lag band, initialized from the regression coefficients. Wires whose Ljung–Box test later comes back white are pruned.
value: Long-range dependencies use compute only where the data statistically requires them, giving long effective context that a same-budget dense-attention transformer has to truncate.

label: g1_loop
name: Misclosure-Retyped Relation Algebra
mech: Attention scores are computed as q_iᵀ R_c k_j. Here c is a relation type chosen by Gumbel-softmax from a codebook of 64 small orthogonal block matrices. During training the model samples token triangles (i,j,k), measures the misclosure ‖R_c(i,j) R_c(j,k) − R_c(i,k)‖, and accumulates it per type triple, as in a surveyor's network adjustment. A type with persistent bimodal misclosure is split into two. A composition that consistently closes onto no existing type creates a new type initialized to the product of the two operators, and types never used in closed loops are deleted. The operators are tiny, so sampling triangles adds under 5% compute.
value: The model builds a closed, compositional vocabulary of relations, which supports multi-hop relational generalization that a same-size transformer's unconstrained attention cannot guarantee.

label: g1_mechneg
name: Contradiction-Annealed Belief Lattice
mech: A frozen small open-weight model parses text into hashed (subject, relation, object) triples. Up to about 500M of these sit in the 32 GB of RAM as integers, each with a truth bit and a pressure counter. Logical constraints are encoded as sparse incidence matrices: transitivity, one value per functional relation, mutual exclusion and type rules. The GPU counts the violated constraints in parallel. A Metropolis process flips truth bits, and its randomness is lowered over time until the total number of violations is at a minimum. To answer a query, the system reads the settled bits and the frozen model writes them out as text. Nothing is learned by gradients, and the GPU work is only sparse integer counting.
value: It keeps a globally consistent belief store with hundreds of millions of facts that reconciles conflicting sources, which a 200M-parameter network can neither hold nor make consistent.

label: g1_mechneg
name: Closure-Merged Rewrite Algebra
mech: The stored objects are edit operators: span-level rewrite transforms taken from aligned sentence pairs, such as a tense change, a negation or swapping roles. They live in RAM as typed diffs. The GPU composes operator pairs in bulk and checks whether each result matches an existing operator class. Classes are kept in a union-find structure that merges, and splits when a merge breaks closure. Generation applies chains of operators to retrieved exemplar sentences.
value: It gives exact compositional and analogical generalization, applying any combination of known transformations to any sentence, instead of the approximate interpolation a same-budget network learns.

label: g1_mechneg
name: Phase-Locked Entity Binding
mech: Each entity and attribute mentioned in a long document gets a complex-valued oscillator, with up to millions of them in VRAM. Links found by a frozen small parser couple them. The GPU integrates the coupled phase equations, which is cheap elementwise work, so linked items fall into phase-locked clusters. Coupling strengths are raised or lowered according to how stably each cluster stays locked over time. To answer a question, the system reads which oscillators share a phase, for example who holds what or where something is.
value: It tracks state and variable bindings across an unbounded document at linear cost, which is where a small fixed-context transformer breaks down.

label: g2_evo1
name: Syndrome-Coded Context Recall
mech: Each 64-token chunk of KV is hashed to a sparse 8192-bit sketch, and only I-chunks are written as codewords into a constraint graph in host RAM; the rate-distortion encoder (distortion = attention-output error on probe queries) decides which chunks earn codeword status. Motion search becomes CPU min-sum decoding: a new chunk's noisy sketch decodes to the nearest stored I-chunk, which is its reference, so search is sublinear over a million tokens. A P-chunk's residual is stored not as low-rank values but as LDPC syndrome bits of its quantized K/V; at read time the GPU uses the motion-compensated reference as side information and decodes the exact quantized cache from the syndrome. Memory capacity therefore follows attention distortion, and the residual rate shrinks wherever the associative memory supplies a good reference.
value: Million-token code or logs stay exactly addressable even when repeated content has been changed (renamed variables, shifted fields), at a few bits per token that fits in 12 GB plus RAM.

label: g2_evo1
name: Loop-Closure Wired Attention
mech: The base model is a 256-token-window transformer whose weight blocks are variables in a square-root information matrix in host RAM, updated with iSAM-style Bayes-tree updates. A candidate long-range "wire" (hidden-state cluster × lag band) is treated like a SLAM loop closure. Its innovation on logged surprisal residuals is tested with a chi-square gate using the Schur complement of the current information matrix, which replaces Bonferroni F-tests. Accepted wires join as new variables: their weights come from back-substitution, and cross-block factors are kept only between blocks a wire connects. Whiteness of innovations (Ljung-Box) also triggers relinearization or removal of a wire, so structure and optimizer state are one sparse factor graph handled by the CPU.
value: Long-range structure is added only where it is statistically needed and is fitted from few tokens, giving data-efficient long context that a first-order dense-attention model on 5B tokens cannot reach.

label: g2_evo1
name: Misclosure-Priced Relational Dispatch
mech: A 200M student scores attention as q·R_c·k over a codebook of 64 orthogonal relation operators, and each step it samples triangles among recent entity tokens and computes loop misclosure. Large misclosure is the dispatch forecast. A dual price λ commits a 4-bit 8B model (paying catch-up prefill and a minimum up-time) only on spans where expected misclosure reduction exceeds λ × cost. On committed spans, the 8B's attention maps between i, j and k are fitted to relation operators. These fits supervise splitting, creating or merging codebook types exactly at the failed loops. As the algebra closes, misclosure and dispatch fall together, so the expensive model ends up teaching only the relations the student cannot yet compose.
value: Near-8B multi-hop relational consistency at small-model cost that keeps falling, because each call to the big model permanently fixes a gap in the student's relation algebra.

label: g2_evo2
name: Loop-Closed KV Smoothing
mech: Context is coded in 64-token chunks: keyframe chunks keep fp16 K/V, and the others store a motion vector (reference chunk plus token alignment) and low-rank residual coefficients. Each chunk is a variable in a sparse square-root information graph kept in fp32 in host RAM. The motion-vector references set which cross-chunk factors exist, and reconstruction factors come from attention-output error on probe queries. When a new chunk's key sketch closely matches a distant chunk, a loop-closure factor is added, and an incremental Bayes-tree update on the CPU re-solves only the affected cliques. It re-codes earlier chunks against the new keyframe and pushes corrected residuals to the GPU. The rate controller reads the marginal covariances: uncertain, heavily attended chunks become keyframes or get higher rank, and well-constrained ones shrink to near-zero residuals. The GPU only reads small residuals and does no extra work.
value: Million-token working memory in 12 GB whose compression error falls as more context arrives instead of building up, which neither a truncating transformer nor a one-pass KV codec can do.

label: g2_evo2
name: Syndrome-Spawned Lag Codes
mech: A 256-token-window base model builds, per position, an 8192-bit signature: which of 1024 k-means hidden-state clusters fired in each of 8 log-spaced lag bands. A sparse parity-check graph in host RAM (10-20 GB of edge lists) is learned from training-corpus signatures with a null-space rule, so valid codewords are typical long-range co-occurrence patterns. At inference, 5-10 rounds of min-sum decoding on the CPU complete the partial signature, and a learned projection adds the completed bands into the residual stream. Syndromes that stay unsatisfied are logged. When a check's violations pass a Bonferroni-corrected Granger F-test against surprisal, the system spawns a single-query wire head over exactly those cluster/band positions, initialized from the regression. Wires that later pass a Ljung-Box whiteness test are pruned, and their pattern is folded back into the code as a new check. All decoding and testing is sparse integer or statistical work on the CPU, overlapped with GPU compute.
value: A small windowed model gets long-range structure recalled and error-corrected from corpus-wide constraint memory, plus exact attention only where tests show it reduces surprisal, so its long-range capacity is not capped by VRAM as a same-budget dense transformer's is.

label: g2_imm
name: Multiple-Time-Step Split Training
mech: A 350M transformer runs a full forward pass every step, but backprops only through its top 3 layers, embeddings and readout. This is the cheap fast force. Every k=4 steps it runs one full end-to-end backward pass, and the gradient for the lower layers is applied as a k-scaled impulse, as in RESPA, with momentum split so the average force stays correct. Lower-layer activations from the fast steps need no stored gradients. That cuts both memory and backward FLOPs, to roughly 1.7 compute units per step instead of 3, so about 1.7× more tokens per week fit on 12 GB.
value: On the same card it trains a larger model on more tokens than a transformer that backprops through the whole stack every step.

label: g2_imm
name: Germinal-Center Clone Memory
mech: A 150M backbone sits beside a repertoire in VRAM of up to 8M clones. Each clone is an int8 64-d receptor plus a sparse 4-token logit payload, about 640 MB in total. At positions where surprisal exceeds a running threshold (the danger signal), the layer-8 state acts as the antigen. Clones that bind it compete, and only the one whose payload most lowers that token's loss is "helped". Helped clones divide, and the mutation noise on their receptors shrinks as their affinity rises. Clones that go unhelped for N presentations die, and clones that keep winning freeze as memory cells. Selection uses only forward passes and integer arithmetic, so capacity grows where the data is surprising at almost no FLOP cost.
value: It stores long-tail facts one-shot and adds capacity on demand, far beyond what 150M gradient-fit weights can hold.

label: g2_imm
name: Ensemble-Kalman Assimilated Memory
mech: A 200M transformer with a 512-token window carries a 32-slot memory from chunk to chunk, kept as 16 perturbed ensemble members that run as batch rows. This is nearly free, because decoding on the RTX 3060 is bandwidth-bound and one read of the weights serves all 16 rows. After each chunk, every member forecasts a summary embedding of it. The actual chunk's embedding is the observation, and a closed-form EnKF update (localized covariance, inflation) moves each member by K(y − Hx). Only the forecast and observation networks are trained, by backprop over short windows. The ensemble spread drives calibration and triggers re-reading, and running it as a smoother lets later evidence revise earlier entity states.
value: It tracks state across long documents while keeping alternative readings alive and reporting its own uncertainty, which a same-budget model with one deterministic state cannot do.
